headline: Baby-Led Weaning vs. Purées
subhead: The two main ways to start solids, compared side by side — and how to pick (or combine) them.
question: What's the difference between baby-led weaning and purées, and which is better?
answer: Baby-led weaning (BLW) means letting your baby self-feed soft, graspable pieces of food from the start, while the purée approach means spoon-feeding smooth mashed food and gradually thickening the texture. Neither is medically "better" — major pediatric groups consider both safe when done with age-appropriate textures and close supervision. Many families combine them. The right choice comes down to your baby's readiness, your comfort with mess and gagging, and what fits your routine.

a.name: Baby-led weaning (BLW)
a.blurb: Baby feeds themselves soft finger foods from the beginning — no purée stage. You offer appropriately sized, soft pieces and let them explore, pick up, and eat at their own pace.

b.name: Purées (spoon-feeding)
b.blurb: You spoon-feed smooth purées first, then move to mashed and lumpier textures, and finally to finger foods. The caregiver controls pace and portion early on.

bestFor.pick: A combination — many families do purées at some meals and finger foods at others

faqs.a: Pediatric guidance considers baby-led weaning safe when your baby shows readiness signs, you offer soft age-appropriate textures and shapes, and you supervise every meal. Learn the difference between gagging (normal) and choking, avoid common choking hazards, and check with your pediatrician before starting.

faqs.q: Which is better for picky eating later?
faqs.a: Evidence is mixed and no method is proven to prevent picky eating. Early, repeated exposure to a variety of flavors and textures — which either approach can provide — is the factor most often linked to broader acceptance.

faqs.q: Can I do both baby-led weaning and purées?
faqs.a: Yes. A combined or 'responsive' approach is common — for example, offering purées at some meals and soft finger foods at others. Babies can move fluidly between the two.

Most guidance points to around 6 months, and readiness signs (sitting with support, steady head control, interest in food, loss of the tongue-thrust reflex) matter more than a fixed date. Your pediatrician can confirm the right time for your baby.

faqs.q: What foods should we avoid at first?
faqs.a: Avoid honey before age 1, choking hazards (whole grapes, nuts, hard raw vegetables, chunks of meat/cheese), and added salt and sugar. Introduce common allergens one at a time and watch for reactions, per your pediatrician's guidance.

disclaimer: This is general educational information, not medical advice. Feeding readiness and safety vary by child — always follow your pediatrician's guidance, and learn infant choking first aid before starting solids.
